extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers querying literary agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing a concise, professional query letter to literary agents for fiction manuscripts, covering tone, content, email practices, and common pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional tone and business-letter format
rubrics_metrics.description: Be professional. It’s a business letter—not a personal letter. Err on the side of caution because formality is never out of place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a businesslike salutation and tone. Avoid overly casual language. Note: salutations that are too impersonal (e.g., “Dear Agent” or “To Whom It May Concern”) are undesirable; and if you have an agent's direct email (e.g., janet@), addressing the query “Dear Agent” looks careless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a referral
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a referral when possible—agents always move referrals to the top of the stack if someone they know vouches for the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat statements like rejection letters, friends’ comments, critique partners’ opinions, paid editors' notes, or conference critiques as referrals—these are not equivalent to a vouch from someone the agent knows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional contact info and email practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Have an email address with your name in it and your own email account; be comfortable with electronic submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a professional address (e.g., SuziWriter@gmail.com), not a shared or cute/personal account (e.g., cutiepiehoneyface@aol.com). Prefer Gmail or Earthlink; avoid AOL because its spam filters can drop messages. Add agents to your safe-senders list so you receive replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start with a rhetorical question
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t start with a rhetorical question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents (especially in NYC) are often sardonic and will not respond the way you expect—openings that pose a rhetorical question are a turnoff. Get straight to the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce the main character immediately by name
rubrics_metrics.description: Get right to the main character—by name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin your query with the protagonist, naming them early so the agent knows who the story centers on rather than languishing in setup or atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise character description
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell who he/she is, and do it in as few words as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tight, specific wording to establish the protagonist's identity/role without long exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the initial point of conflict/inciting incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell what happens to him or her—the initial point of conflict in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the inciting incident or the event that starts the plot so the agent understands the book’s premise and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show choices, consequences, and high stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Show two choices the main character faces as well as the consequences of those choices. The stakes must be high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the protagonist’s dilemma and why it matters—what are the meaningful options and outcomes? Convey strong stakes to make the premise compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the phrase 'Fiction novel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase is redundant (a novel is fiction) and makes the writer sound ignorant—avoid unnecessary labels that reveal poor industry awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming 'Surefire bestseller.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not declare the work a “Surefire bestseller.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the agent decide market potential; self-proclaimed bestseller claims come across as arrogant and uninformed about the industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming 'Film potential.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents may not be film agents and claims about film potential are presumptuous—focus the query on what the book is about rather than extraneous, speculative media tie-ins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude inspiration/backstory from the query
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include how you came up with the idea or the inspiration for the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You likely have only about 250 words—don’t waste them on origin stories. Agents want to know what the book is about, not the process of invention: “It’s the equivalent of making sausages; I do not want to see you do it.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep queries concise (approx. 250 words)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You have limited space; prioritize plot, character, stakes, and essential credentials. Avoid long-winded exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrelevant personal information; include only relevant author credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include irrelevant personal details (where you live, number of pets). Only include work/personal information if it is directly relevant to your authority to write the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your occupation or background uniquely qualifies you to write this book, include that, but be cautious—sometimes practitioners (e.g., cops, doctors) make poor fiction writers because their familiarity can stifle storytelling. Omit trivial personal facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: don't query too soon; better to wait until ready
rubrics_metrics.description: You can query too soon; you cannot query too late.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the query letter as the foundation of your publishing career—ensure your manuscript and query are ready before submitting, rather than rushing to query prematurely.
